newsitem.title: CHINA: China courts hear more intellectual property cases.
newsitem.headline: China courts hear more intellectual property cases.

text.p: Chinese courts are dealing with a rising number of cases involving intellectual property rights, but more training is needed to ensure judicial expertise and ethics, the China Daily said on Thursday.
Courts dealt with 493 property rights cases involving computer software in the first 10 months of 1996, up 36.9 percent year on year, the official newspaper said in a front page report.
State media has in recent weeks trumpeted victories in the war against copyright pirates who churn out audio-visual and computer products.
The propaganda blitz appears designed to blunt criticism from other countries, particularly the United States, that Beijing is not doing enough to clamp down on intellectual property rights abuse.

Southern Guangdong province has reported closing down more than 20 underground compact disc production lines in less than a month as part of a national anti-pornography campaign that officials say also nets copyright pirates.

In the first 10 months of last year, Chinese courts heard 341 cases involving copyright, up 6.2 percent compared with 1995, and handled 251 cases of trademark infringement, up 22 percent, China Daily said.

The courts intended to step up protection of intellectual property rights this year and more than 3,000 judges had been trained to try such cases, it quoted Li Guoguang, vice-president of the Supreme People's Court as saying.
An important task was to educate judges in professional ethics and to be true to the law, Li said.
U.S. indignation at widespread copyright piracy in China took the two countries to the brink of a multibillion dollar trade war last year.

Western computer and music industry executives believe a Chinese crackdown on pirates has had some success since the signing of a Sino-U.S. accord that averted trade war, but they say many counterfeit production lines remain in operation.
